definition: A chatbot (originally chatterbot) is a software application or web interface designed to converse through text or speech, functioning as a conversation partner.
details: Chatbots have existed for decades, but chatbots based on deep learning have gained popularity during the AI boom of the 2020s, with the releases of generative AI (GenAI) chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Grok. These chatbots typically use fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) to generate text. A major area where chatbots have long been used is customer service and support, with various sorts of virtual assistants.

explainer.lead: A chatbot lets people converse with software through ordinary text or speech. It can rely on simple keyword matching or a fine-tuned large language model, and it is widely used for customer support, information sharing, and other conversational tasks.

tiers.eli5: A chatbot is like a desk clerk inside a computer: you write or speak to it, and it writes or speaks back. An early chatbot could notice the word “mother” and reply with a prepared question about your family. Newer ones can create their answers after learning from enormous amounts of text.
tiers.practitioner: Choose the implementation to fit the task: ELIZA and A.L.I.C.E. used pattern matching, while ChatGPT-style systems generate text with fine-tuned LLMs. Deployments include messaging apps, company websites, and internal service desks, with scripted sequences using triggers, user responses, and decision trees for predictable workflows. Fluency should not be treated as proof of understanding, since ELIZA demonstrated how easily superficial processing can create that illusion.
tiers.paperLevel: In plain notation, r_t = f(u_t, c_t): a chatbot maps the current user turn u_t and conversational context c_t to a text or speech response r_t, using anything from pattern matching to a transformer-based LLM trained on a large text corpus. Joseph Weizenbaum published ELIZA in 1966; it recognized clue words and returned prepared responses without a claim of genuine intelligence. Its central limitation was superficial processing, while the Turing test separately concerns whether conversational content alone lets a judge distinguish a program from a human.

explainer.example: If an ELIZA-style bot receives “I want to talk about my mother,” it can spot the clue word “MOTHER” and answer, “TELL ME MORE ABOUT YOUR FAMILY.” The reply moves the conversation forward, but it comes from pattern matching rather than demonstrated understanding.

usedIn.name: Customer service
usedIn.detail: Banks, airlines, retailers, and other organizations use chatbots to answer simple questions and provide a first point of contact.

usedIn.name: Facebook Messenger
usedIn.detail: Developers gained chatbot support in 2016; 30,000 bots appeared in six months, rising to 100,000 by September 2017.

usedIn.name: Healthcare
usedIn.detail: Physicians in one study expected benefits for scheduling appointments, locating clinics, and providing medication information.

usedIn.name: Walmart Canada
usedIn.detail: In 2021, a chatbot negotiated contract terms with suppliers in a trial involving 89 businesses.

explainer.intuition: A chatbot is a conversation loop: receive a person’s message, work out a response, and return it as text or speech. The main design choice is whether that response comes from prepared patterns and rules or is generated by a language model.
howItWorks: Receive a user’s text or speech through an app, website, or messaging service.
Interpret the turn using clue-word patterns, a decision tree, or a language model.
Use conversation context and, in some integrations, web search or image-generation tools.
Produce the next reply and continue the exchange.
explainer.whyItMatters: Chatbots give people a conversational way to obtain information and services without requiring a human for every exchange. Their evolution from ELIZA to LLM-based assistants also shows why convincing conversation and genuine understanding should not automatically be treated as the same thing.
misconceptions: Not every chatbot uses an LLM; early systems relied on pattern matching and prepared responses.
A fluent reply does not by itself establish intelligence or genuine understanding.
Chatbots are not a 2020s invention: ELIZA was published in 1966.
Customer support is important, but chatbots are also used internally, in healthcare, and in negotiations.
